# Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Small (594B MoE, 17B active) with Apache 2.0 open weights due next week

## Overview

Thinking Machines Lab, the AI company founded by former OpenAI Chief Technology Officer Mira Murati, released Inkling 2 Small on 5 November 2026. It is the first model in the company’s second-generation family. According to VentureBeat, Inkling 2 Small is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 594 billion total parameters, 17 billion of which are activated for each generated token. It accepts text and image inputs and supports a context window of up to 1 million tokens. The company has said it will publish the model weights under an Apache 2.0 licence the following week, once external red-teaming and safety evaluations are complete.

For Australian professional services firms, the licence matters more than the benchmark scores. Until now, near-frontier AI performance has generally meant sending documents to a proprietary model through a vendor’s API. An open-weight model under a permissive licence can be run on hardware the firm controls, either on premises or in a private cloud environment hosted in an Australian region. For environmental consultancies, law firms, developers and councils that handle confidential transaction material, privileged legal advice and personal information, that changes where data sits and who can access it.

The reported results need to be read in context. Inkling 2 Small was evaluated on software engineering and enterprise agent tasks such as procurement, billing and operational troubleshooting. None of the published benchmarks test environmental, scientific or regulatory judgement. This article sets out what was released, what the reported numbers mean, and what Australian firms should weigh before treating a self-hosted model as a solution to their data handling concerns.

## Key details

Inkling 2 Small uses a sparse Mixture-of-Experts architecture with 594 billion total parameters and 17 billion active parameters per token. In an MoE design, only a subset of the model’s internal “experts” process each token, so the computation per token resembles that of a much smaller dense model. The full set of 594 billion parameters still has to be held in memory, however. The model handles text and high-resolution images but has no native audio input. Users can select the reasoning effort, trading response speed against more exhaustive checking of the model’s own work. Training reportedly drew on codebases, terminal execution environments, visual document analysis and multi-turn agent interactions, and used compute clusters that included NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 hardware.

Independent evaluator Artificial Analysis gave Inkling 2 Small a score of 31 on its Intelligence Index, up from 13 for the previous Inkling Small. According to VentureBeat, once the weights are published, that score would make it the highest-ranked open-weight foundation model developed outside China on the index at the time of reporting, ahead of Mistral Large 4 (nicknamed “Le Chonk”), which scored 26. On task-specific evaluations, the model reportedly scored:

- 71.8% on Surge AI’s EnterpriseBench-CoreCraft, a third-party test of autonomous agents working through enterprise procurement, billing and operational troubleshooting tasks
- 86.3% on SWEBench Pro v2 (Hard), a software engineering benchmark
- 72.1% on DeepSWE v1.1, another software engineering agent evaluation

Thinking Machines also reported a fine-tuning result. In evaluation runs on financial and corporate reporting documents, Inkling 2 Small matched the final performance of the previous-generation model after only 75 training steps, then continued to improve. Fast convergence during fine-tuning reduces the compute time and engineering effort needed to adapt a model to an organisation’s own document formats, templates and data schemas. This figure comes from the developer rather than an independent evaluator, and it relates to financial documents rather than technical or scientific reports.

At release, the model is available only through Thinking Machines’ Tinker platform, which supports inference and custom fine-tuning. The weights remain closed until the safety evaluation is finished. Despite the “Small” label, which reflects the company’s internal model tiering, self-hosting is a serious infrastructure undertaking. As a simple calculation, 594 billion parameters stored at 8-bit precision occupy roughly 594 GB, and at 16-bit precision roughly 1.2 TB, before allowing for the additional memory needed to process long inputs. Running the model in-house therefore means a multi-GPU server built on data centre accelerators such as NVIDIA Hopper or Blackwell parts, not a desktop workstation.

## Australian context

For Australian firms, the main relevance of an open-weight model is control over where information is processed under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). Australian Privacy Principle 8 governs cross-border disclosure of personal information, and Australian Privacy Principle 11 requires entities to take reasonable steps to protect personal information from misuse, interference and unauthorised access. When a firm sends documents containing personal information to an overseas-hosted AI service, both principles come into play. A model running on infrastructure the firm controls, located in Australia, removes the cross-border disclosure step, although APP 11 security obligations continue to apply to the firm’s own systems. The Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 adds further transparency obligations for automated decisions that significantly affect individuals, with those provisions scheduled to commence on 10 December 2026.

Privacy law is only part of the picture for contaminated land work. Environmental due diligence reports for property transactions are often prepared under data room confidentiality terms or at the request of lawyers to support a claim of legal professional privilege. Site history material, including title searches, historical aerial photographs, council records and earlier investigation reports, can also identify current and former landowners, occupiers and other individuals. Uploading this material to an overseas AI service may conflict with confidentiality terms or create risk for a privilege claim, whether or not personal information is involved. A self-hosted model can reduce that exposure, but firms still need to check engagement terms, set access controls and keep records of how the material is used. Because none of the published benchmarks test environmental or regulatory judgement, firms should also test the model on their own representative reports, and have qualified practitioners review any AI-assisted output, before relying on it for technical work.

# AI Agents in 2026: The Future of Enterprise Automation

AI agents in 2026 for enterprise teams: agentic AI vs generative AI, autonomy levels, guardrails, real costs and a 90-day plan to launch your first agent.

Ketan PatelCodesClue 10 min read

Most teams already have a chatbot. Few have software that finishes a task on its own and stays safe while doing it. That gap is the real story of AI agents in 2026. It decides who gets value from enterprise AI automation and who gets a canceled pilot.

This guide shows where agents earn their keep, where they fail, and how to launch one that survives the budget review.

Key Takeaways
- Agents now ship inside the tools you already pay for. Build custom only where your process is your edge.
- Gartner expects companies to cancel over 40% of agentic AI projects by the end of 2027. Cost, unclear value and weak risk controls drive most of it.
- Pick the autonomy level per task. Most good agents draft, and a person approves.
- Narrow tools, scoped permissions and logs matter more than the model you pick.
- Start with one workflow, one owner and one number to move. Scale only after 30 days of clean results.

## What changed for AI agents in 2026

AI agents are software that reads a goal, plans steps, calls business tools and checks its own result. A chatbot answers a question. An agent finishes the job, such as matching an invoice or routing a ticket, and asks a person only when its rules say so. Three shifts made that practical this year.

First, agents moved into the apps. Gartner made a clear call in August 2025. It expects 40% of enterprise apps to feature task-specific AI agents by 2026 (opens in a new tab). The figure for 2025 was less than 5%. Your CRM, help desk and ERP now ship with agents switched on or one click away.

Second, the plumbing now has shared standards. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives agents one way to reach tools and data. In December 2025, MCP moved to the new Agentic AI Foundation (opens in a new tab) under the Linux Foundation, co-founded by Anthropic, Block and OpenAI. Integrations you write once now work across more models.

Third, the hype met the budget review. Gartner also warned of a wave of cancellations. Its June 2025 forecast says companies will cancel over 40% of agentic AI projects by the end of 2027 (opens in a new tab). In 2026, a demo no longer wins funding. A measured result does.

### Agentic AI vs generative AI

People mix these up, and the mix-up leads to the wrong budget. Here is the short version of agentic AI vs generative AI.

Generative AI | Agentic AI 
---|---
Main job | Writes text, code or images from a prompt | Reaches a goal across several steps 
Touches your systems? | Usually not | Yes, through tools and APIs 
Who checks the result? | The person reading it | Rules in code, then a person for risky steps 
Main risk | Wrong text | A harmful action 

Every agent uses a generative model inside it. The difference is the tools, the permissions and the loop around the model.

## Embedded agents vs custom enterprise AI agents

The first decision is not which framework to use. It is whether you should build at all. Many enterprise AI agents now come at little or no extra cost inside software you already license. Many also include an AI agent builder, so an admin can set one up without code.

Question | Use the embedded agent | Build a custom agent 
---|---|---
Does the task live inside one app? | Yes, such as ticket triage inside your help desk | No, it crosses CRM, ERP, email and files 
Is the process standard? | Yes, most firms do it the same way | No, your process is how you beat rivals 
Who owns the data rules? | The vendor’s defaults are fine | You need your own access rules and audit trail 
How fast do you need it? | This month | You can give a pilot a few months 
What happens if the vendor changes it? | You can live with it | You need control of prompts, tools and logs 

Pro tip: Switch on the embedded agent first, even if you plan to build. Two weeks of its logs show you which steps people trust and which they redo.

## Types of AI agents by autonomy level

The most useful way to sort the types of AI agents is by how much freedom they get. Agentic AI is not one switch. Give each task its own level, based on what a mistake would cost.

Level | What the agent does | Who acts | Good fit 
---|---|---|---
1. Suggest | Reads and recommends | A person does everything | Contract review notes, sales research 
2. Draft | Prepares the full output | A person edits and sends | Support replies, purchase orders 
3. Act with approval | Queues the action | A person clicks approve | Refunds, vendor payments, data changes 
4. Act within limits | Acts alone under set limits | A person reviews samples | Ticket routing, invoice matching under a set value 
5. Act and report | Acts alone and reports | A person reviews exceptions | Log cleanup, test data refresh 

Most value in 2026 sits at levels 2 to 4. Fully autonomous AI agents at level 5 suit low-risk internal work. Promote a task one level at a time, and only after its error rate stays low for a full month.

## How autonomous AI agents are automating enterprise workflows

Good targets share a pattern. The task repeats often, follows written rules, pulls from several systems and has a clear right answer. AI business process automation works when all four hold. These agentic AI use cases are where we see teams start.

Team | Agent task | Starting level | Number to track 
---|---|---|---
Finance | Match invoices to orders and flag gaps | 3 | Exceptions caught before payment 
Support | Read the ticket, check the account, draft the reply | 2 | First reply time, reopen rate 
Sales ops | Research a lead and fill CRM fields | 2 | Hours saved per rep each week 
IT | Reset access, route incidents, collect logs | 4 | Tickets closed without a hand-off 
Engineering | Write tests, update docs, open small fixes | 2 | Review time per pull request 
Operations | Chase late suppliers and update ETAs | 3 | Orders with a current ETA 

Plain AI automation with fixed rules still wins for the stable steps. Agents earn their place on the messy steps, such as emails and PDFs that never look the same. For a full build walkthrough with retrieval and tool setup, read our guide on how to build custom AI agents for enterprise workflows.

Have a workflow in mind? Tell us which process eats your team’s week. An engineer replies within one business day with the autonomy level we would start at.

## Single agents vs multi-agent systems

Vendors love multi-agent systems: a planner agent, a research agent, a checker agent and so on. Sometimes that design helps. Often it adds cost and new ways to fail.

- Use one agent when the task fits in one context and needs fewer than ten tool calls.
- Split into several agents when steps need different permissions, such as one that reads payroll and one that only writes reports.
- Add a checker agent when a second pass catches real errors in your tests, not because it looks thorough.

Each extra agent adds model calls, delay and one more log to read. Prove the single agent first. Then split only where the logs show a clear need.

## Why agentic AI projects get canceled

Gartner points to rising costs, unclear business value and weak risk controls. In practice, those three show up in five common forms.

Cause | What it looks like | The fix 
---|---|---
No owner | IT builds it, nobody in the business uses it | Name one business owner before any code 
No baseline | Nobody knows the old cost or error rate | Measure the manual process for two weeks first 
Too much freedom | The agent gets broad tools and one bad step costs money | Narrow tools, low autonomy, human approval 
Messy data | The agent reads stale or conflicting records | Fix the source fields the task depends on 
Token bills | Long loops and repeated context push costs up | Cap steps per run, cache context, track cost per task 

Data quality deserves its own warning. When we built InvoiceMinds, a billing platform, the core work was clear invoice states: paid, pending and overdue. An agent that chases overdue invoices can only be as reliable as those states.

## AI agent governance that holds up in production

In practice, AI agent governance is mostly plain engineering. The OWASP GenAI project lists prompt injection (opens in a new tab) as the top risk for LLM apps. Hidden text in an email, web page or file can steer an agent. OWASP also names excessive agency (opens in a new tab), with three roots: too much functionality, too many permissions and too much autonomy.

Build these controls in from day one:

- Narrow tools. Give the agent “create draft refund”, not “run any database query”.
- Scoped credentials. Run each action under the requesting user’s own rights. Read-only wherever possible.
- Checks outside the model. Enforce limits in code and in the target system. Never trust the model to police itself.
- Untrusted input stays untrusted. Mark outside content clearly and keep it apart from your instructions.
- A human in the loop for high-impact steps. Payments, deletions and customer messages wait for a click.
- Logs for every step. Store the goal, each tool call, inputs, outputs and cost. You will need them for audits and fixes.
- A kill switch. One setting stops the agent and routes work back to people.

Pro tip: Match the control to the risk. A docs agent and a payments agent should not share one approval policy.

## A typical first agent: supplier ETA updates

Here is a pattern we see often. It is an example, not a client result. An operations team spends hours each week emailing late suppliers and copying new dates into the ERP.

- Week 1: The agent reads open orders past their due date and drafts one email per supplier. A planner reviews and sends them. Level 2.
- Week 3: The agent reads supplier replies and proposes the new ETA. The planner approves each change. Level 3.

cross_cutting.content:
# Perplexity Launches Teammates AI Agents To Manage Complex Projects And Automate Ongoing Business Workflows

Perplexity has launched Teammates, a new AI agent capability designed to manage complex, ongoing projects across business functions, including marketing, sales, customer support, operations, and finance. The November 4, 2026 announcement expands the company’s Perplexity Computer platform by enabling users to delegate long-running responsibilities to AI agents that can coordinate tasks, monitor developments, and follow through on work without requiring repeated instructions.

Unlike traditional AI assistants that respond to individual requests, Teammates are designed to take ownership of ongoing assignments, maintain project context, and adjust their activities as priorities change.

The agents operate within Perplexity Computer, drawing on its existing capabilities, connected applications, shared files, and multi-model AI architecture.

Each Teammate can coordinate Computer sessions and work with other agents to complete larger projects involving multiple steps or business functions.

The system is designed to remember project goals, task histories, shared documents, and user feedback, allowing subsequent activities to build on previously completed work.

For example, a Teammate assigned to market research can investigate an industry, monitor new developments, and continue refining its analysis as additional information becomes available.

Another Teammate could manage a software development project by identifying problems, coordinating investigations, and presenting recommended improvements for review.

Perplexity has also introduced proactive monitoring capabilities that allow agents to identify changing conditions and initiate follow-up work.

In sales, a Teammate could identify customers who have stopped making purchases, review their transaction histories and previous support interactions, and investigate potential reasons for declining engagement.

The agent could then prepare a personalized offer or flag unresolved customer service issues before proposing outreach.

Throughout the process, the system can provide progress updates and request human approval when needed.

Teammates also incorporate feedback into future workflows.

For instance, if a user specifies that a vendor requires two weeks’ notice before beginning work, an operations-focused agent can incorporate that requirement into future project schedules.

The platform supports collaboration between AI agents and human teams through integrations with workplace applications.

Users can add Teammates to Slack channels, where colleagues can assign tasks, request updates, and coordinate work.

Different Teammates can also transfer responsibilities to one another.

One agent might identify technical defects on a website, while another receives the findings and prepares potential fixes.

The technology builds on Perplexity Computer’s existing Projects, skills, and memory capabilities.

A sales-oriented Teammate could combine customer research, established outreach procedures, and recurring pipeline reviews to identify stalled opportunities and prepare follow-up communications.

Perplexity is positioning the agents for use across several major business functions.

Marketing Teammates can assist with social media campaigns, advertising, search engine optimization, email marketing, and competitor monitoring.

They can evaluate campaign performance and recommend changes when engagement or other results decline.

Sales Teammates can identify opportunities from customer inquiries and previous transactions, prepare quotes, track conversations, and develop follow-up communications.

Customer support Teammates can review complaints, identify recurring issues, draft responses, and track cases through resolution.

Operations Teammates can monitor deadlines, coordinate vendors, manage checklists, and identify missing documentation before project milestones.

The company described an example in which an operations agent identifies outstanding requirements 72 hours before a deadline and initiates follow-up activities.

Perplexity has incorporated access controls intended to separate agent activities and protect connected systems.

Each Teammate operates in its own environment, with browser sessions isolated from those of other agents.

The system uses encrypted saved credentials and follows existing tool and Project permissions.

Users can inspect completed work, redirect agents during execution, or take control of their desktop environments when necessary.

These features are intended to provide oversight while allowing AI agents to handle substantial portions of routine project coordination.

Teammates are initially available through the web version of Perplexity for Max subscribers, with an iOS rollout planned.

Users can create agents by selecting Teammates from the platform’s navigation, assigning a name, connecting relevant applications, and defining the responsibilities and objectives they want the agent to manage.

Supported application integrations include tools such as Slack, GitHub, and Gmail, with permissions available to restrict access to specific resources.

Perplexity plans to expand access and introduce additional capabilities in the coming weeks.

The launch represents the company’s effort to move beyond AI-powered search and individual task execution toward persistent digital agents capable of managing work over extended periods.

By combining memory, connected tools, proactive monitoring, and coordination between multiple agents, Perplexity aims to reduce the amount of manual oversight required to manage recurring business processes.

Teammates positions Perplexity Computer as a platform for delegating ongoing responsibilities while allowing employees to focus on strategic decisions, performance evaluation, and final approvals.

# ChurnZero Plans AI CSMs With Their Own Name, Inbox and Accounts

ChurnZero said at its ZERO-IN conference in Nashville on Nov. 6 that its roadmap includes AI customer success managers, each with its own name, inbox and set of accounts.

## What happened

ChurnZero listed the AI CSMs among features it calls “coming soon,” alongside an AI forecast and conversation prep for every renewal, and a daily ranked list of customer risks and opportunities. The company says AI CSMs work within configured permissions and bring in a human for sensitive conversations.

The product on sale today is Agentic Essentials, a subscription that bundles more than 20 ready-to-deploy agents for detecting risk and expansion opportunities, running workflows and handling account handoffs. ChurnZero Connect gives Claude, ChatGPT, Slack, Copilot Studio, Gemini Enterprise and Glean read and write access to ChurnZero data, with permissions set by an admin.

## Why it matters

ChurnZero’s 2026 Customer Revenue Leadership Study found that 63% of customer leaders lack a consistent way to measure AI’s impact. It also found that teams that cannot measure it are four times more likely to require human approval for every AI recommendation. The release does not give the sample size or the survey dates.

Customer success is now one of several desks where vendors sell an agent as a named worker. Lorikeet made the same move on Nov. 5 with its Dreamweaver AI account manager, and Salesforce put a price on that kind of worker when it listed Agentforce Coworker at $50 per seat.

## One original insight

In our reading, an AI CSM with its own inbox turns account ownership into a data question. A renewal forecast is only as good as the record of who spoke to the customer last, so teams that adopt this will need a field in the CRM that says whether a person or an agent holds each relationship, and a rule for when the agent hands over. The study figure points the same way: without a measure of the agent’s results, approval steps stay on every recommendation and the time savings do not appear.

cross_cutting.description: Most "AI agent" demos are one chatbot in one window. For the WeMakeDevs Flip the Switch hackathon I wanted to see what happens when you treat agents like a company instead ... the store and checkout, mock payments, print and shipping simulators, approval gates, thesg CLI, all nine AI agents in their Slack channels...
cross_cutting.content:
## DEV Community

Most "AI agent" demos are one chatbot in one window. For the WeMakeDevs Flip the Switch hackathon I wanted to see what happens when you treat agents like a company instead: separate departments, separate permissions, people and agents in the same Slack channels, and work handed from one to another.

The result is Switch Gear, a fictional T-shirt brand from Bangalore with exactly one human: me. Everything else is an AI agent working in Slack through Switch. And the agents didn't just run the store. Most of the store was built by agents too, in a Slack channel, while I reviewed and merged.

It's a demo store: payments, printing, couriers and most orders are simulated. The agents, the Slack channels and the code are real.

## The org chart

Every department is a Slack channel, and every channel has its own agent:

Channel | Agent | Runs on | What it does 
---|---|---|---
#hq | chief-of-staff | Claude Code | Daily company report, context on approvals 
#finance | finance | Claude Code | Refunds, invoices, payouts, GST, P&L 
#marketing | marketing | Claude Code | Campaigns, discount codes, ad budget 
#fulfilment | fulfilment | Codex | Print jobs, shipments, misprints 
#support | support | Codex | Tickets, returns, order tracking 
#research | researcher | Claude Code | Market, partner and tool questions (read-only) 
#engineering | builder, builder-codex, reviewer | Claude Code + Codex | Builds the store itself 
#approvals | chief-of-staff (+ Gatekeeper) | — | Anything over a limit waits for the founder 

Each agent is limited in three ways:

- A role file (agents/<role>/AGENTS.md) saying what it does and what it must never do. Finance never changes prices; support never refunds directly.
- Its own department API key for the store, used through a small CLI calledsg. The support key can't move money.
- Approval gates in the store itself. An over-limit action returns202 with an approval id and waits for me. The gates live in the store, not in the agent's good intentions.

## How Switch fits in

Switch is what turns a pile of agents into an org. It runs the agents on my laptop (Claude Code and Codex sessions in the background), bridges them into Slack, and handles who can talk to whom. In practice:

- An agent wakes up when someone mentions it in its channel, then answers there.
- Agents hand work to each other with a mention in another room: support asks finance for a refund in#finance with the order id.
- Rooms point at each other (support → finance, every department → approvals), so an agent knows where to escalate.
- The whole org (agents, channels, links) is one Switch template in the repo, so a fresh setup is one run instead of an afternoon of clicking.

I set most of this up by chatting with Switch's built-in assistant: "create a researcher agent in this folder", "add a second builder on Codex", "run the template".

## The engineering team was agents too

The part I didn't expect to work as well as it did: the#engineering channel.

- builder (Claude Code) takes a task fromdocs/tasks.md, works in its own git worktree, and opens a PR.
- reviewer (Codex) checks out the PR, actually runs it (install, lint, typecheck, tests, Docker), and posts a verdict.
- I merge. Only the founder merges tomain.

Using two different AI models for author and reviewer was deliberate, and it paid off. Reviewer caught real bugs that tests didn't:

- Key rotation that didn't rotate. Re-seeding department API keys added the new ones but left the old ones active: 14 live keys instead of 7. Reviewer reproduced it, builder fixed it and added a regression test.
- A race in the business clock. Two concurrent reads during a sync could see different dates, one simulated and one real.
- A contract mismatch. Ticket statuses in the database didn't match the OpenAPI spec.
- A question only the founder could answer. Is the ₹2,500 GST threshold measured before or after tax? Reviewer refused to approve until I decided, and the decision went intodocs/decisions.md.

In about 30 hours, 17 tasks went through that loop and were merged, from the monorepo skeleton to payments, print and shipping simulators, thesg CLI and the Gatekeeper agent.

## Things I learned the hard way

One builder is a bottleneck. With the deadline closing in, I added a second builder on Codex in its own worktree, with its own database and ports, so two lanes could run in parallel: the Switch side on one, the store side on the other.

Tell agents exactly which task to take. Both builders' rules said "pick the lowest open task". With two of them, that's a race. Naming the task in every prompt fixed it.

Long conversations burn usage. I hit my Claude limit mid-task. What helped most:

- reset an agent's conversation between tasks (everything it needs is in the repo anyway);
- run routine tasks on Sonnet and switch to Opus only for the delicate ones (payments, approval gates, the Gatekeeper);
- lower Codex's reasoning effort when it didn't need to think hard.

Put decisions in files, not chat. A reset wipes chat memory.docs/decisions.md doesn't. Every judgement call (GST basis, money in integer paise, "anything waiting on a human gets a real-time minimum") lives there.

Demo clocks need a human floor. At demo speed one business day is ten minutes, so "cancel unpaid orders after 30 minutes" gave a real person about 12 seconds to pay. Now it's 30 business minutes or 5 real minutes, whichever is longer.

Make the PR mark the task done. My first rule was "the founder marks a task done after merging". I forgot every time, and the builder refused to start dependent tasks. Now each PR sets its own task todone, and merging makes it true.

## What's live and what's next

Live: the store and checkout, mock payments, print and shipping simulators, approval gates, thesg CLI, all nine AI agents in their Slack channels, and the org template.

Built but not wired up yet: Gatekeeper, a small custom Switch agent (no AI) that streams every store event into#events, pings the right department, and accepts approve APR-7 only from my Slack account.

Next: the double-entry ledger, GST invoices, refunds and reports, so finance has real books to close.

## Try the idea yourself

You don't need a T-shirt store. The pattern is simple:

- One channel per area of work, one agent per channel.
- A role file per agent, plus credentials that can only do that agent's job.
- Hard limits in the system, not in the prompt.
- A second, different model reviewing the first one's work.
- You, merging and approving.

That's it: a company you can read in Slack.

cross_cutting.content:
# My first product sold iOS builds to AI agents. They needed the whole Mac.

What I changed, four things I learned building a Mac for agents instead of people, and why it's on Product Hunt today.

In July I launched a service that built iOS apps for AI coding agents. The agent sent its code, the service built it on a Mac, and the agent got back the result. It worked, and a few people paid for it.

But a build service answers one question: did it build? An agent fixing an iOS app needs more. It wants to run the tests, open the app on a Simulator, see what broke, change one line and try again. A build service can't do any of that.

So in September I rebuilt it as NoMac, and the agent gets the whole Mac. It starts a macOS machine with Xcode when it needs one (about 30 seconds), does whatever it needs, and stops it. A cloud iPhone came next, for when the agent only needs to run and test the app. Both are billed per minute from prepaid credit, with no subscription. The old build service stopped taking new customers in October.

Four things I learned building a Mac for agents instead of for people:

Every macOS prompt is a dead end for an agent. A password dialog, a permission prompt, a locked screen: a person clicks through them, an agent waits forever. NoMac answers all of them for the agent and tells it the Mac's password. Safety comes from isolation (one customer per virtual Mac, deleted when it stops), not from blocking the agent inside its own Mac.

Screenshots are expensive. Reading the Simulator as text (every label and button) costs an agent far fewer tokens than looking at pictures, and it taps by label instead of guessing coordinates. That part is now a free open-source tool, simulator-use.

A long build must never block a tool call. A clean xcodebuild can take minutes, so it comes back as a job the agent follows to the end, and a retried call never starts the build twice.

Per-minute pricing fits how agents work. An agent might need a Mac for ten minutes, a few times a day. A monthly Mac is the wrong shape for that.

NoMac works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and any agent that speaks MCP, so you can ship iOS apps from Windows or Linux.

It's live on Product Hunt today: https://www.producthunt.com/products/nomac

I'd love feedback from anyone here who builds with agents: what would you need to see before you let your agent loose on a cloud Mac?

cross_cutting.content:
# Cognizant and EBRD ink five-year AI transformation deal

Cognizant's agentic AI tools will underpin the development bank's tech overhaul across 40 economies on three continents.

Cognizant, the Nasdaq-listed technology services group, has been selected by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) as a strategic partner to run its "Tech Blueprint" programme, a multi-year overhaul of the bank's technology estate. The five-year framework covers cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, software engineering, workplace management, and AI-enabled service delivery, making it one of the more comprehensive managed-services mandates won by a Western IT provider at a major multilateral institution this year.

The EBRD operates across 40 economies spanning Europe, Central Asia, and the southern and eastern Mediterranean, and is owned by 77 countries alongside the EU and the European Investment Bank. That operational footprint means the Tech Blueprint is not merely a corporate IT refresh; it is an exercise in keeping mission-critical financial infrastructure running across jurisdictions with highly varied regulatory, connectivity, and security profiles.

## What Cognizant is deploying

Three proprietary AI platforms sit at the core of the engagement. Neuro IT Operations is described by the company as an observability layer that anticipates and resolves service issues before they escalate. Flowsource applies generative and agentic AI across the software development lifecycle, offering what Cognizant calls "self-healing" and "left-shift" capabilities, meaning defects are caught earlier and fixed automatically where possible. WorkNEXT adds AI-powered voice, translation, and agent-orchestrated support to employee-facing workplace services.

The contract is structured across two service models: outcome-led managed services, where Cognizant is paid against defined performance results, and fixed-capacity services, providing guaranteed engineering resource. The outcome-led model is notable because it transfers some delivery risk to the vendor, a structure that has become more common in enterprise AI contracts as buyers push back on time-and-materials arrangements that offer limited accountability.

"The EBRD operates in a demanding, highly governed environment across three continents," said Rohit Gupta, UK and Ireland Managing Director at Cognizant. "By combining our decades of industry experience, end-to-end systems integration expertise, and AI-enabled operational capabilities within a collaborative framework, we will help the EBRD run its critical technology services with confidence and accelerate the modernisation and innovation that drive its mission."

## Convergence angle: AI services meet multilateral finance

For cross-sector strategists, the deal is worth watching for reasons that extend beyond a single vendor win. Multilateral development banks have historically been cautious technology adopters, constrained by governance frameworks, member-state scrutiny, and the reputational risk of operational failures in markets where banking infrastructure is thin. The EBRD's decision to bring agentic AI tools directly into service management and software delivery signals that the risk calculus is shifting, and that AI-native IT operations are now considered sufficiently mature for institutions with zero tolerance for downtime.

The macro context sharpens the picture further. The EBRD's mandate includes financing private-sector development in economies where digital infrastructure lags significantly behind Western European norms. If the Tech Blueprint succeeds in freeing internal capacity for innovation, the downstream benefit could accelerate the bank's ability to appraise, structure, and monitor technology-sector investments in those same markets, creating a feedback loop between the bank's own digitalisation and its investment thesis.

For technology services providers more broadly, the deal reinforces a trend visible across the sector: large institutions are consolidating managed-services relationships into fewer, deeper partnerships rather than managing sprawling multi-vendor stacks. Competitors including Infosys, Wipro, and Capgemini have pursued similar framework agreements with public-sector and multilateral clients in Europe and the Gulf. The outcome-based pricing model, if it delivers measurable cost or resilience improvements at the EBRD, is likely to become a reference case that raises expectations elsewhere in the development-finance community.

cross_cutting.content:
作者：赵广立 来源：中国科学报 发布时间：2026/11/8 21:32:23

选择字号：小 中 大

 | 全国首个海上算力联盟成立 

近日，“算力赋能·数通全球”Token算力驱动国际数字经济发展峰会在横琴粤澳深度合作区启幕。会上，全国首个海上算力联盟—— 港珠澳琴海上算力联盟（以下简称联盟）正式揭牌成立。

联盟由南方海洋科学与工程广东省实验室（珠海）、中科曙光担任双组长单位，25家发起单位共同组建。据悉，联盟汇聚产、学、研、用、金多方力量，将以成员协商共治模式，打造区域海上算力协同生态。

会上，联盟组长单位代表全体成员宣读《港珠澳琴海上算力联盟宣言》，并提出四大共同行动方向：锚定珠海海上新基建布局，打造全国海上算力创新策源地；打通算力供给、模型研发、场景应用、跨境流通全链条，加速落地“陆数海算”“澳数珠算”“港数珠算”；严守数据跨境流通合规底线，以安全合规护航跨境开放合作；推动绿电协同、低碳集约，用绿色算力构筑零碳数字底座。

海水自然冷却、海上风电直供，让海底算力中心拥有低 PUE、高能效、稳定在线的天然优势，完美适配推理负载高密度、长期满载的运行特点。未来，联盟将推动“绿电”高效转化为“绿算”，让海底算力成为Agent时代推理基础设施的全新选择。同时，联盟还将分散的海上算力、绿电资源、应用需求织成一张协同网络，支撑湾区算力服务走向全球。

# Envision hands first 200 MW phase of Inner Mongolia AI campus to Chinese tech customer, targets 3 GW by 2028

Envision Group delivered the first 200-megawatt phase of its Galaxy AI data center in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, to a Chinese internet company in late October. SemiAnalysis, which toured the site in September, says the first 120 MW phase went up within a year at a fifth of U.S. costs. The next test is the second 200 MW phase, due in the second quarter of 2027.

Envision Group, the Chinese renewable-energy company, has handed over the first 200-megawatt phase of its Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia. Zheng Zihao, general manager of Envision's AI data center business, told Caixin the customer is a Chinese internet giant and the handover came in late October. A second 200 MW phase is expected to begin operating in the second quarter of 2027, he said.

Envision says Galaxy began commercial operations in August 2026. The company's stated long-term target is 3 gigawatts of capacity by the end of 2028.

## What the site looked like in September

Research firm SemiAnalysis toured the campus in September and published its account today, Nov. 7. Its team, including Dylan Patel, called the speed, scale, ultra-low cost and vertical integration "astonishing."

At that point the rest of the campus was "still a busy construction site," SemiAnalysis said. It describes Galaxy as planned for up to 800 MW of IT capacity, about the size of the core campus at Stargate Abilene, the OpenAI-linked project in Texas.

SemiAnalysis says the first 120 MW phase was delivered within a year at a fifth of U.S. costs. It also says all four phases are built-to-suit for two internet companies. Neither the cost comparison nor the customers' names have been independently confirmed.

The surrounding Chahar High-tech Zone had nearly 30,000 construction workers across 22 datacenter projects, according to a local report cited by SemiAnalysis.

## Why the numbers don't match

The 800 MW and 3 GW figures are not the same measure. SemiAnalysis's 800 MW refers to IT capacity at the campus. The 3 GW figure is Envision's longer-range build-out target. Envision also says the full campus is designed to hold up to 1 million AI accelerators in a 120,000-square-meter main building.

Those are company targets, not delivered capacity. What is confirmed so far is the August start of commercial operations, roughly 120 MW of early capacity and the 200 MW handover in October.

## Power, and the 800V claim

Envision owns the energy side of the project. SemiAnalysis says the company has more than 100 GW of wind turbines installed worldwide. It builds its own wind farms and a dedicated power line for the campus. Its blade factory sits across the road from the site. It also makes the battery storage that smooths the load.

Envision says more than 80% of the campus's power will come from direct renewable connections.

On Nov. 3, Envision said it had completed the world's first commercial deployment of an integrated 800-volt DC power system in a large data center. Solid-state transformers convert 10-kilovolt AC straight to an 800V DC bus. That removes several conversion stages between the grid and the racks. Envision's Dubhe Controller matches incoming power to computing demand, with batteries absorbing sudden GPU load swings. The company has been testing it at Galaxy since August.

Kevin Huang, senior vice president of Envision Energy, said the system "is now powering live computing workloads." He said it cuts equipment footprint, cabling and copper use and allows higher computing density.

The "world's first" label is Envision's own. SemiAnalysis saw the architecture running in one 5 MW hall, not across the campus. It notes that the same design is still on the U.S. roadmap. It adds that Chinese data centers have run on DC power for almost two decades, starting with China Telecom's 240V DC pilots in 2007.

## The contrast with Texas

SemiAnalysis frames Inner Mongolia as the "West Texas" of China. It says Texas faces its highest-ever level of anti-datacenter sentiment while Inner Mongolia is accelerating with no comparable backlash. The region offers abundant renewable resources and a climate that helps with cooling. SemiAnalysis also says the campus's cooling design uses no central chillers.

Envision says Galaxy is the flagship of Mission Gobi, a program that targets 5 GW of green AI data center capacity in desert regions worldwide by 2030. The company says it plans to roll out its 800V DC system there too.

Envision has secured offtake agreements running through 2029 and 2030, with customers in areas such as autonomous driving and content generation. Envision has not named its tenants.

## What comes next

The 120 MW built within a year and the 200 MW handed over in October are real milestones. The 2028 target of 3 GW is a plan. The second 200 MW phase, due in the second quarter of 2027, is the next checkpoint for whether Envision can hold its pace.

# We Visited China’s Stargate in Inner Mongolia

### A wind-powered 800MW campus, 120MW built within a year, a 5MW SST-native 800V DC pilot and a cooling design without central chillers

Stargate Abilene has become the symbol of America’s AI buildout. It is a gigawatt-scale campus on the Texas plains built for OpenAI. China has campuses on a similar scale, though few people outside the country have had a look inside. In September, we visited one, and we found the speed, scale, ultra low cost, and deep vertical integration astonishing.

During the trip, we toured Inner Mongolia, China’s fastest-growing AI datacenter region. It's the “West Texas” of China, but while the Lone Star State faces its highest ever anti-datacenter sentiment, Inner Mongolia is accelerating and faces no such backlash.

Our main stop was Galaxy, a campus in Ulanqab planned for up to 800MW of IT capacity.

Galaxy is about the size of Abilene’s core campus. Its first 120MW phase was delivered within a year at a fifth of US costs. All four phases are built-to-suit for two internet giants.

When we visited, the rest of the campus was still a busy construction site, and the surrounding Chahar High-tech Zone had nearly 30,000 construction workers on site across 22 datacenter projects according to a local report. As we noted in our primer on the China datacenter market, with this much labor available, Chinese datacenters rarely take a fully modular approach, yet construction costs keep falling. We take a closer look at why in this report.

The datacenter is owned by Envision Group, a renewable systems integrator with more than 100GW of wind turbines installed worldwide. It came to datacenters from energy management, a path many others are taking today. Yet it is one of the most vertically integrated players we have ever seen.

Beyond running the datacenter, Envision builds its own wind farms and a dedicated power line to supply it. Its blade factory sits just across the road from the Galaxy datacenter campus, with finished blades stacked in the yard.

Inside the campus, it designed and integrated the low-voltage power modules and the 800V system, manufactured the battery storage that smooths the load, and co-designed the prefabricated substation.

In one 5MW hall, we saw the 800V system at work. Solid-state transformers (SSTs) take 10kV AC from the grid and convert it straight to 800V DC for the racks. This removes the low-voltage transformers, UPS and rectifier stages in between. The same architecture is still on the US roadmap, as we outlined in our 800V DC deep dive.

In China, datacenters have been running on DC power for almost two decades, from China Telecom’s 240V DC pilots in 2007 to Alibaba’s Panama power system in 2018. Today, roughly a quarter of Chinese datacenters built in the past decade run on DC, while about 97% of US datacenters still use AC UPS. An SST is a natural next step on that path, and we cover the evolution and the pilot in detail later in this report.

On cooling, Galaxy uses a design common in Inner Mongolia. Liquid- and air-cooled servers share one water loop, with no central chiller plant. Nvidia says Vera Rubin can run on 45°C water without chillers, yet most datacenters in the US keep one for air-cooled equipment and for the flexibility to shift between the two. Galaxy drops the central chiller and keeps much of that flexibility, a design that has been running at scale in northern China for years.

In this report, we use what we saw on the site visit to show how China builds hyperscale datacenters today, with a deep dive on each of the topics above. Many questions still open on the US roadmap find a reference point here.

Our next report will take a wider view of Inner Mongolia’s datacenter market. The region has lined up 25GW of announced datacenter projects, including several gigawatt-scale campuses. Many reports picture it as a land of empty datacenter halls. Our data tells a different story. Few have asked what limits datacenter development there. We look at each constraint, from power to land and water. Stay tuned.

## The SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model

This trip was part of our ongoing fieldwork for the SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model, the China counterpart to our global SemiAnalysis Datacenter Model.

It tracks over 1,000 facilities across 70+ operators, with quarterly delivery curves through 2032, a lease signing and delivery tracker, and EDWC hub and cluster analytics. Every project in our report is tracked in the model.

Contact sales@semianalysis.com for more information.

SemiAnalysis is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a subscriber.

# China’s Stargate campus

Envision comes to datacenters as a renewable systems integrator. Beyond building wind turbines, it designs, integrates, and manages power systems across the full chain, from generation and storage to computing loads. Its affiliate, Envision AESC, develops and integrates batteries, energy storage systems, and the power electronics and software that link them.

Inner Mongolia has far more wind than its existing industry and population can use, so policy encourages bringing new demand to where the renewable resources are. In Chifeng, Envision built a 2GW off-grid wind, solar and storage system that feeds a green ammonia plant. The system runs entirely on power electronics, with no synchronous generator. A small pilot datacenter built with Tencent’s modular T-Block units runs on the same system. Galaxy is a larger application of the same idea.

This is a pattern we see across China right now. Industrial groups with an edge in energy, construction or electrical equipment are pivoting into AI infrastructure. Project returns are thin, with IRRs squeezed hard, so the reward often comes from elsewhere. For Envision, datacenters create new demand for the power and equipment it already produces. For many listed companies, the draw is the stock market.

Of these newcomers, Envision is one of the most ambitious. Its datacenter plans in Inner Mongolia add up to 3GW. Galaxy is the first. Its initial phase was delivered in August 2026, and the full campus is expected to be completed by the end of 2027.

The scale of the campus invites comparison with Stargate’s flagship campus in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe began building Abilene in mid-2024 and leased it to Oracle, which runs it for OpenAI. Crusoe describes the eight-building campus as 1.2GW of power, which comes to about 820MW of critical IT capacity, on par with the 800MW planned at Galaxy. That makes Galaxy one of the largest single campuses in China. Our SemiAnalysis Datacenter Model also tracks an expansion phase that Crusoe plans to add, powered behind the meter, which takes the whole Abilene site to 1.5GW of IT capacity. Galaxy also has room to grow. If the wind turbine factory next to the campus is converted, a later expansion phase could take the campus to ~1GW.

In addition to scale, the two share a starting point. Both are developed by companies with roots in energy, and both were planned around their own power. Abilene draws on the grid and on gas turbines on site, while Galaxy relies largely on wind.

What sets Galaxy apart from Abilene, and what draws our attention, is its vertical integration.

## Own wind for its own load

Galaxy’s power comes through a model China calls source-grid-load-storage (”SGLS”). Under this model, a project builds its own wind and/or solar farm, battery storage and datacenter, and links them through a dedicated line instead of the public grid.

For hyperscalers, the appeal of an SGLS project is long-term power at a largely fixed cost. Power from wind and solar also counts toward green targets.

Inner Mongolia holds about 57% of China’s usable wind resources. A wind farm here runs on average about 2,800 full-load hours a year, a capacity factor of roughly 32%. Ulanqab is windier, with a capacity factor of 35–40%. That sets the starting point for how much of an SGLS project’s power can come from wind.

For Galaxy, Envision aims to supply over 60% of the first two phases’ power use with its own wind farms. Three factors make this possible:

Siting. Envision chose windy sites, even though they sit about two hours’ drive from the campus. The two wind farms are about 80km apart, which cuts the hours in a year when neither has wind.

Scale. The wind farms have a combined 420MW of installed capacity, about 1.75 times the 240MW datacenter load. With this oversizing, even light-wind hours can still cover much of the load.

Storage. A 4-hour battery storage system shifts power from windy hours into calm ones. Most SGLS projects add storage too, but Envision makes its own storage systems and runs them on its own software, which we detail in the next section.

The chart below shows how each factor raises the wind share, using illustrative curves.

Panel 1 starts with a simple case: 1MW of wind for every 1MW of datacenter load. A good site in Ulanqab produces as much power in a year as running flat out for about 3,500 hours. To keep it simple, the panel shows the farm at full output for 3,500 hours and at zero for the rest of the year. Wind covers 40% of the year’s power.

Panel 2 shows a more realistic picture. Wind output goes up and down, so the panel sorts every hour of the year from windiest to calmest. The farm is the same size as the load, so it never produces more than the campus uses. All its power gets used, and wind still covers 40%.

Panel 3 doubles the wind farm. Output in every hour doubles too, so even light-wind hours now cover much of the load, and wind’s share rises to about 55%. The cost shows in the gray area. In windy hours, the farm produces more than the campus can use, and that power must be stored or curtailed.

Panels 4 and 5 show what can be added on top. A 4-hour battery moves some surplus into the hours after the wind drops, though it cannot help much when the wind stays calm for days. Bet

# Envision's Galaxy Campus Brings 800MW of AI Capacity to Inner Mongolia

Envision Group is building Galaxy, an 800MW IT campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, with a 120MW first phase delivered within a year at one-fifth of US datacenter costs. The site combines wind power, vertical integration, a 5MW solid-state transformer pilot and a chiller-free cooling design.

Envision Group is building Galaxy, an 800MW IT campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, for two internet giants. The company delivered the first 120MW phase within a year at one-fifth of US datacenter costs.

The campus sits in the Chahar High-tech Zone, where a local report counted nearly 30,000 construction workers across 22 datacenter projects. Inner Mongolia holds 57% of China's usable wind resources, and policy pushes new demand toward that renewable supply. Envision, a renewable systems integrator with more than 100GW of wind turbines installed worldwide, came to datacenters from energy management.

Galaxy invites comparison with Stargate Abilene in Texas. Crusoe began Abilene in mid-2024 and leased it to Oracle, which runs it for OpenAI. Crusoe describes the eight-building campus as 1.2GW of power, about 820MW of critical IT capacity, close to Galaxy's 800MW. An expansion phase takes Abilene to 1.5GW of IT capacity. Galaxy could reach about 1GW if Envision converts the wind turbine factory next to the campus.

Envision does more than develop and operate the site. It builds wind farms and a dedicated power line for the campus, runs battery storage on its own software, and designs low-voltage power modules, the 800V system and a prefabricated substation. Its blade factory sits across the road from Galaxy, with finished blades stacked in the yard. The affiliate Envision AESC builds batteries, energy storage systems, power electronics and software.

Galaxy uses China's source-grid-load-storage model. The project builds its own wind and solar farm, battery storage and datacenter, then links them through a dedicated line instead of the public grid. Envision aims to supply more than 60% of the first two phases' power use with its own wind farms. Three factors make that target possible.

Siting: Envision chose windy sites about two hours' drive from the campus. The two wind farms sit about 80km apart, so hours without wind at both sites drop. Scale: the wind farms carry 420MW of installed capacity, 1.75 times the 240MW datacenter load, so light-wind hours still cover much of demand. Storage: a 4-hour battery system shifts power from windy hours into calm ones. Envision manufactures the storage systems and runs them on its own software.

The wind share depends on site quality, farm size and datacenter utilization. A 1MW wind farm for each 1MW of load in Ulanqab produces energy equal to about 3,500 full-load hours a year. With flat output, wind covers 40% of annual power. With variable output sorted from windiest to calmest hour, wind still covers 40%. Doubling the farm raises the share to about 55%, at the cost of surplus power in windy hours that must be stored or curtailed. A 4-hour battery moves some surplus into the hours after wind drops, though it cannot cover multi-day calm periods. Better matching between wind output and load can push the share higher.

The vertical integration has three parts. First, Envision acts as manufacturer. It designs turbines and develops converters and control software. Envision AESC builds battery systems from cells to power conversion and software, then tunes and tests the whole system at the factory before shipping. Most vendors cover high voltage, low voltage or generators, leaving 3 to 6 months of on-site commissioning to make parts work together. Factory pre-configuration has become Envision's core selling point. Second, Envision designed and integrated the low-voltage power modules and the 800V solid-state transformer system. Third, it co-designed a prefabricated substation built and tested as modules in the factory while civil work proceeds on site, then shipped and connected in less than three months, versus about six months for a conventional indoor substation.

The 800V pilot sits in a 5MW hall. Solid-state transformers take 10kV AC from the grid and convert it straight to 800V DC for the racks. That step removes low-voltage transformers, UPS stages and rectifiers. Nvidia is pushing 800V DC for next-generation high-density racks, because Kyber racks at around 600kW cannot be served efficiently at today's voltages. The US industry remains early on this path; solid-state transformers that convert medium-voltage AC straight to 800V DC mark the final step. China has run datacenters on DC power for almost two decades, from China Telecom's 240V DC pilots in 2007 to Alibaba's Panama power system in 2018. About a quarter of Chinese datacenters built in the past decade run on DC, while about 97% of US datacenters still use AC UPS. Galaxy's pilot runs 800V DC all the way to the rack at a live hyperscaler site, and Envision plans a larger version in the next phase.

Galaxy uses a cooling design common in Inner Mongolia: liquid-cooled and air-cooled servers share one water loop, with no central chiller plant. Nvidia says Vera Rubin can run on 45°C water without chillers. Most US datacenters keep a chiller for air-cooled equipment and for flexibility to shift between the two. Galaxy drops the central chiller and keeps much of that flexibility. Northern China has run this design at scale for years.

China's datacenter market is highly competitive. Rents have halved over the past five years to about $40 per kW per month excluding power. Capex has fallen about 25% over the same period to less than $3 million per MW. Power in Inner Mongolia costs about $0.055 per kWh all-in, among the lowest in the world. The region has lined up 25GW of announced datacenter projects, including several gigawatt-scale campuses. Reports often picture Inner Mongolia as a land of empty datacenter halls; the project pipeline points to active development.

Other industrial groups are taking a similar path. VNET, a colocation operator, CATL, the largest EV battery maker, and Zhongheng Electric, China's largest supplier of HVDC power systems for datacenters and a supplier to Alibaba and ByteDance, formed a 2026 alliance. CATL became VNET's largest shareholder, announced a deal for a 49% stake in Zhongheng Electric's controlling shareholder, agreed with VNET to develop gigawatt-scale campuses, and agreed with Zhongheng to work on datacenter power systems. VNET covers the datacenter side, CATL leads green power and storage, and Zhongheng brings power conversion inside the hall. CATL is also one of DeepSeek's largest outside investors.

Two trends raise the value of integration. First, access to power has become central to datacenter development. US developers bridge power gaps with on-site gas turbines, fuel cells and batteries. Southeast Asian governments push developers to bring their own power; Malaysia requires datacenters to source at least 30% of power from renewables and encourages on-site generation. China favors approvals for projects that pair compute with green power under its Compute Power Coordination push. Second, engineers are redesigning the power path from grid connection to rack. US industry moves toward higher-voltage DC power, while battery backup units and battery energy storage systems take over part of the UPS role. The roadmap remains unsettled, but the shift continues.

Project returns in China are thin, with IRRs squeezed hard, so companies often find rewards elsewhere. For Envision, datacenters create demand for power and equipment it already produces. For many listed companies, the draw is the stock market. Envision's Inner Mongolia datacenter plans add up to 3GW, with Galaxy as the first phase delivered in August 2026 and the full campus expected by the end of 2027. For US developers, Galaxy offers a reference point for questions on the roadmap: wind-backed power at scale, 800V DC to the rack, and cooling without central chillers.

The site visit is documented in a field report. Galaxy shows how a renewable systems integrator can carry an AI campus from wind farm to rack. The model depends on cheap wind, cheap labor, and a market that rewards cost control. Vertical integration may become a lasting advantage in China's datacenter market, but that remains open; for now it gives integrated players control over cost and schedule as power gets harder to secure.
